title: Envy of Heaven
credits: World and reconstruction: Epocheye.
People: bodies, skin, eyes and hair from MakeHuman and MPFB assets (CC0). Clothes made for Epocheye.
People's walk, idle and talk: motion by Quaternius, Universal Animation Library (CC0), adapted to these figures.
Bullock cart: model created with Meshy (meshy.ai), simplified for the web. CC BY 4.0 (creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0) if made on Meshy's free plan.
You, the restorer: body and animation by Quaternius, Universal Animation Library (CC0), recoloured.
Tamarind tree: Tree Small 02 by Rico Cilliers, Poly Haven (CC0).
Palm trees: made for Epocheye.
Surfaces: textures from Poly Haven (CC0), Epocheye's own photographs, and pattern tiles used in the reconstruction.
Voices: synthetic, made with Kokoro (hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Apache 2.0).
Titles set in Anton (SIL Open Font License 1.1).
Physics: Rapier by Dimforge (Apache 2.0).
The rooms you step into are Epocheye's panoramas of the palace:
Exterior colours after James Hunter, watercolour of the north front, February 1792. Yale Center for British Art, Paul Mellon Collection, B1974.12.1168. Public domain (CC0).
Interior wall texture derived from a photograph by Mike Prince, CC BY 2.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tipu_Sultan%27s_Summer_Palace_(16414465309).jpg
Painted ceiling pattern after Epocheye's own photograph of the surviving ceiling, September 2026. Its extent across the upper floor is inferred.
Present-day surfaces from Epocheye's own photographs, September 2026.
Where paint survives today is not mapped; NOW shows plain surfaces.
The projecting front balcony is not shown, because its projection is unrecorded. The balcony viewpoint stands at the front arcade of the upper floor.
Evidence image: James Hunter, watercolour of the north front of the palace at Bangalore, February 1792. Yale Center for British Art, Paul Mellon Collection, B1974.12.1168. Public domain (CC0).

Evidence image: Robert Home, "Inside View of the Palace at Bangalore", engraved by Lowry, published 1 February 1794, in Select Views in Mysore (London: R. Bowyer, 1794). Scan: National Library of Norway. Public domain.
Evidence photographs of the palace today (the front, a painted wall panel, a painted ceiling): Epocheye, September 2026.
Textures and sky: Poly Haven, CC0.
Today's surroundings beyond the palace garden are not modelled and are shown as haze.
Narration: synthetic voice.
Office desks, shelves and chests: built in code for Epocheye.
_note: Hand-written open-world layer. Positions are Blender metres [x, y]. Story beats are referenced by id from story.json and never copied. A dialogue line that states a fact carries a fact id from story.json or world_facts.

world_facts.claim: Bullock carts were the standard transport of the Mysore country. Where these carts stand is our guess.
world_facts.source: Epocheye's period world log, row 16: type medium confidence, position none

world_facts.claim: The avenue through the fort is drawn on Mackenzie's survey of March 1791. Its width is not stated.
world_facts.source: Mackenzie survey, March 1791 (RCIN 735001), as traced in the fort project

world_facts.claim: Mackenzie's survey of March 1791 marks three tanks of good water inside the fort. Their depth, their stone edge and the look of the water are our reconstruction.
world_facts.source: Mackenzie survey, March 1791 (RCIN 735001), key 11, as traced in the fort project

world_facts.claim: Robert Home's account of 1794 calls the solid body of the fort's rampart red clay. The rampart was faced with stone.
world_facts.source: Robert Home, Select Views in Mysore (1794), quoted in the Bangalore Fort evidence ledger (bangalore-fort/research/evidence.md), section 5

world_facts.claim: The fort had two gateways: the Delhi Gate on the north and the Mysore Gate on the south.
world_facts.source: Home (1794), Wilks, Rice (1897) and Fortescue (1902), as compared in the Bangalore Fort evidence ledger, section 3

world_facts.claim: Robert Home, 1794: the fort's ditch was "deep, and wide, but dry in most parts of it". Its width and depth are not recorded.
world_facts.source: Robert Home, Select Views in Mysore (1794), quoted in the Bangalore Fort evidence ledger, sections 6 and 11

world_facts.claim: Mackenzie's survey of March 1791 names the granaries inside the fort, within a walled inclosure. Their heights are not recorded.
world_facts.source: Mackenzie survey, March 1791 (RCIN 735001), key 12, as read in bangalore-fort/research/magicwindow-build-record.md, section 12d.2

world_facts.claim: Mackenzie's survey of March 1791 marks work yards for smiths, carpenters and other artificers inside the fort.
world_facts.source: Mackenzie survey, March 1791 (RCIN 735001), key 13, as read in bangalore-fort/research/magicwindow-build-record.md, section 12d.2

world_facts.claim: Palanquins at the palace are our reconstruction of court transport. Hunter and Home show none here.
world_facts.source: Epocheye's period world log (TSP_period_assumptions.md), row 19: low confidence

world_facts.claim: This durbar is staged from Buchanan's account of how the court worked. No record describes a durbar on this day, and no record says which balcony the ruler used.
world_facts.source: Our staging of F12 and R2; Epocheye's period world log (TSP_period_assumptions.md), rows 9 and 22

world_facts.claim: The clerks, desks and ledgers shown here are our reconstruction. The records say the principal departments were in the palace from 1831, not how the rooms were laid out.
world_facts.source: Our staging of F14; no record of the layout of the offices has been found

world_facts.claim: Where Hunter's records lie in this world is our placement. Where he stood to draw is not fixed on this map, and the front he painted is not the front modelled here.
world_facts.source: Fact M2; Epocheye's period world log (TSP_period_assumptions.md), row 10 and 'Left out, and why'

npcs.placement_note: Where he stands is our placement. No record puts a sentry on this spot.

d-carpenter.speaker: carpenter
d-carpenter.text: You want to know what holds this place up? Teak.
d-carpenter.say: You want to know what holds this place up? The teak does.

d-carpenter.speaker: carpenter
d-carpenter.text: The pillars, the arches, the beams, the ceilings. All wood.

d-carpenter.speaker: carpenter
d-carpenter.text: Ask the mason about the rest. Masons always say it is all stone.

d-mason.speaker: mason
d-mason.text: Look down. Every pillar stands on a stone base.

d-mason.speaker: mason
d-mason.text: The outer walls? Mud, under the plaster.

d-mason.speaker: mason
d-mason.text: The rest is further on. Take the cart, it is a long walk.

d-carpenter-m2.speaker: carpenter-m2
d-carpenter-m2.text: You again. Still staring at the front?

d-carpenter-m2.speaker: carpenter-m2
d-carpenter-m2.text: Colour is not my trade. Ask me about wood.

d-carpenter-m2.speaker: carpenter-m2
d-carpenter-m2.text: Smiths, carpenters, all the trades have their work yards inside this fort.

d-carpenter-m2.speaker: carpenter-m2
d-carpenter-m2.text: Want a picture of it? Find someone with time. I have none.

d-sepoy.speaker: sepoy
d-sepoy.text: Careful at the edge. It is a long way down.

d-sepoy.speaker: sepoy
d-sepoy.text: Two gates into this fort. The Delhi Gate to the north, the Mysore Gate to the south.

d-sepoy.speaker: sepoy
d-sepoy.text: Look at the ditch. Deep and wide, and dry in most parts.

d-sepoy.speaker: sepoy
d-sepoy.text: This wall looks like stone all the way through. Inside, it is red clay.

d-sepoy.speaker: sepoy
d-sepoy.text: Go on down. The palace is the pretty part.

d-grain-trader.speaker: grain-trader
d-grain-trader.text: Mind the bags. They are heavier than they look.

d-grain-trader.speaker: grain-trader
d-grain-trader.text: The granaries are inside the fort, behind their own wall.

d-grain-trader.speaker: grain-trader
d-grain-trader.text: On a durbar day we are allowed into the open court.
d-grain-trader.say: On a darbar day, we are allowed into the open court.

d-grain-trader.speaker: grain-trader
d-grain-trader.text: The court has fountains, to cool the air.

d-bearer.speaker: bearer
d-bearer.text: Please step around. We have only just set it down.

d-bearer.speaker: bearer
d-bearer.text: My shoulders know every road in this fort.

d-bearer.speaker: bearer
d-bearer.text: The highest officers get a balcony, at each end of the court.

d-bearer.speaker: bearer
d-bearer.text: The lower officers have the hall under the ruler's balcony.

d-bearer.speaker: bearer
d-bearer.text: Us? We wait out here with everybody else.

d-mason-m3.speaker: mason-m3
d-mason-m3.text: See these columns? They rise as high as the roof of the upper storey.

d-mason-m3.speaker: mason-m3
d-mason-m3.text: On a durbar day, nobody like us goes up there.

d-mason-m3.speaker: mason-m3
d-mason-m3.text: But you are not from here. Go on.

d-clerk.speaker: clerk
d-clerk.text: Not there, please. That pile is in order.

d-clerk.speaker: clerk
d-clerk.text: The principal departments of the government sit in this palace now.

d-clerk.speaker: clerk
d-clerk.text: A palace is a strange place to keep ledgers.

d-clerk.speaker: clerk
d-clerk.text: Somebody has mixed up these dated papers. Put them in order for me, will you?
